paper_title: SpanCalib-VLM: Calibrated Hallucination Span Detection in Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Detecting hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) requires both accurate span localization and well-calibrated confidence scores. Fine-tuned generative VLMs excel at identifying hallucinated text spans but suffer from overconfidence and high inference latency. Discriminative sequence taggers offer deterministic speed and superior calibration but exhibit conservative span recall. We present SpanCalib-VLM, a hybrid dual-system for the SHROOM-Visions Shared Task that combines a multimodal sequence tagger, consisting of XLM-RoBERTa-Large fused with a SigLIP vision encoder via cross-attention, with our fine-tuned generative VLM (Qwen3.5-4B-SHROOM-SFT). Through a Union-Calibrated Fusion strategy, candidate spans from the generative model are re-scored with calibrated probabilities from the sequence tagger. On the SHROOM-Visions English evaluation split, our ensemble achieves a Pearson calibration correlation of 0.41 and an overall IoU of 0.39, with a clean-response IoU of 0.91} and overall detection accuracy of 70.7%. We make our model weights and code publicly available.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Detecting hallucinations in Large VisionLanguage Models (LVLMs) requires both accurate span localization and wellcalibrated confidence scores. Fine-tuned generative VLMs excel at identifying hallucinated text spans but suffer from overconfidence and high inference latency. Discriminative sequence taggers offer deterministic speed and superior calibration but exhibit conservative span recall. Through Union-Calibrated Fusion strategy, candidate spans from the generative model are re-scored with calibrated probabilities from the sequence tagger. On the SHROOM-Visions English evaluation split, our ensemble achieves Pearson calibration correlation of 0.413 and an overall IoU of 0.391, with clean-response IoU of 0.913 and overall detection accuracy of 70.7%. We make our model weights and code publicly available.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) such as GPT-4V, Qwen-VL (Bai et al., 2023), and MiniCPM-V (Yao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025) have made remarkable progress in visual question answering and multimodal reasoning. However, they regularly produce visual hallucinations: text that misdescribes scenes, invents objects, or mischaracterizes attributes (Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). The SHROOM-Visions shared task (Mickus et al., 2024; Vazquez et al., 2025) targets finegrained hallucination detection, requiring systems to (i) identify character-level span boundaries of hallucinated segments and (ii) provide well-calibrated probability scores evaluated via Pearson correlation. Existing approaches fall into two paradigms. Generative VLM fine-tuning trains autoregressive models to output structured span annotations; these achieve high span IoU but suffer from overconfidence and high latency (up to 23 per sample with chain-of-thought). Discriminative sequence tagging applies token-level classifiers that run in single forward pass with well-calibrated outputs, but produce conservative span boundaries. SpanCalib-VLM bridges this gap through four contributions: 1. multimodal sequence tagger combining XLM-RoBERTa-Large with SigLIP-2 vision features via cross-attention, equipped with multi-task heads for span detection, probability calibration, and error categorization. 2. Union-Calibrated Fusion, an ensemble algorithm that uses generative VLM spans as candidate proposals and re-calibrates them with the taggers probability distribution. 3. Competitive results on SHROOM-Visions: Pearson 0.413, IoU 0.391, and 91.3% clean detection accuracy. 4. Public release of model weights, code, and evaluation artifacts.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Hallucination in VLMs. Benchmarks such as POPE (Li et al., 2023), CHAIR (Rohrbach et al., 2018), and MME (Fu et al., 2025) evaluate hallucination at the sentence or object level. The SHROOM series (Mickus et al., 2024; Vazquez et al., 2025) raises the bar by requiring token-level span identification paired with probability calibration, joint localization-anduncertainty problem. 1 https://github.com/Aman-byte1/ Hallucination-Detection-in-LVLMs Calibration. Modern neural networks and pretrained language models exhibit severe miscalibration and overconfidence, particularly under domain or distribution shift (Desai and Durrett, 2020; Ovadia et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2017; Kadavath et al., 2022). Standard posthoc calibration methods like temperature scaling and Platt scaling adjust global logit temperature but fail to capture fine-grained, tokendependent span uncertainty. Rather than relying on uncalibrated autoregressive generation probabilities, our approach equips the discriminative tagger with dedicated MSE regression head to directly supervise token-level confidence against continuous human consensus ratios.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.content: In this section we elaborate on our approach. Figure 1 illustrates the overall architecture of our SpanCalib-VLM system.

sections.title: Tagger
sections.content: Text encoder. We use XLM-RoBERTaLarge (Conneau et al., 2020) (24 layers, dh = 1024). The input concatenates the prompt and response as Question: Tp nResponse: Tr and is tokenized to maximum of = 512 tokens, yielding hidden states Htext RN dh. Vision encoder & cross-attention fusion. Image features are extracted with SigLIP 2 (Zhai et al., 2023), producing patch embeddings R196768, which are linearly projected into the text hidden space (Vproj R196dh). Cross-attention then fuses visual context into language representations: Hfused = LayerNorm Htext + Softmax (cid:18) (cid:18) QK dh (cid:19) (cid:19) (1) https://hf.co/google/siglip-base-patch16-224 Multi-task heads. Three parallel heads operate on each token hi: 1. Span classifier (Headspan): 2-layer MLP σ(), predicting binary hallucination probability ˆyi [0, 1]. 2. Probability calibrator (Headcalib): 2layer MLP σ(), predicting continuous calibration score ˆpi [0, 1]. 3. Category classifier (Headcat): 2-layer MLP softmax(), predicting error type among five categories. Training objective. The composite multitask loss is: = LBCE(ˆy, y) + λ1LMSE(ˆp, p) + λ2LCE(ˆc, c) (2) with λ1 = 1.0 and λ2 = 0.5. The MSE term directly supervises probability calibration against annotator agreement scores p. The auxiliary classification loss LCE acts as multi-task regularizer, forcing shared encoder representations to capture fine-grained semantic category boundaries.

sections.title: 3.3 System 2: Generative VLM
sections.content: We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B (Yang et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026) via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on SHROOM-Visions training data (Mickus et al., 2026) to produce structured JSON spans. From System 2s output, candidate spans SVLM are converted into binary character mask MVLM(k) {0, 1}.

sections.title: 3.4 Union-Calibrated Fusion
sections.content: Neither system alone optimizes both localization and uncertainty estimation: System 2 provides high span recall through deliberative generation but outputs uncalibrated scores, while System 1 provides well-calibrated probabilities but conservative span boundaries. Our fusion algorithm operates as follows: 1. Extract candidate span boundaries SVLM from System 2. 2. Map System 1s token probabilities to character-level array PSC(k) via subtoken offset alignment across the full response sequence. 3. Compute the probability-guided ensemble score: Pens(k) = w1 PSC(k) + w2 MVLM(k) (3) with w1 = 0.55, w2 = 0.45. The weights w1 and w2 were selected via hyperparameter grid search on the validation set: assigning slightly higher weight to System 1 Input: Image + Prompt Tp + Response Tr System 1: XLM-R-Large + SigLIP-2 System 2: Qwen3.5-4B-SFT Headspan Headcalib Headcat PSpanCalib(k) (prob. distribution) MVLM(k) (binary mask) Union-Calibrated Fusion: Pens(k) = 0.55 PSC(k) + 0.45 MVLM(k) Calibrated Spans + Probabilities + Categories Figure 1: SpanCalib-VLM architecture. System 1 (discriminative tagger) produces calibrated token probabilities; System 2 (generative VLM) proposes candidate spans. Union-Calibrated Fusion combines both into final predictions. (w1 = 0.55) anchors score magnitudes to its superior calibration baseline (Pearson 0.369 vs. 0.285), while w2 = 0.45 allows System 2s binary mask MVLM(k) {0, 1} to act as spatial proposal weight for candidate span positions.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Data. We fine-tune models on 15,102 samples of multilingual dataset in EN, FR, IT, and ZH (cf. Table 8), evaluating main baselines on the English validation split and cross-lingual performance across all four languages on validation (cf. Table 7) and test sets (cf. Table 2). Training. SpanCalib-VLM is trained for 5 epochs on NVIDIA A40 GPUs with AdamW (η = 1.5105), linear warmup (10%), batch size 16, and max sequence length 512. Table 5 summarizes key hyperparameters. Training Dynamics Table 9 tracks validation metrics across epochs. Pearson correlation peaks at epoch 2 (0.3688); subsequent epochs exhibit overfitting, with training loss continuing to fall while validation loss rises. The bestcheckpoint strategy based on validation Pearson successfully preserves the optimal state.

sections.title: 5.1 Main Results
sections.content: Table 1 compares standalone baselines and our full system. SpanCalib-VLM achieves the highest Pearson correlation (0.413) and overall IoU (0.391) on the English evaluation split (N = 379), with clean-response IoU of 0.913 and detection accuracy of 70.7%. While 0.413 Pearson represents validation performance, official shared task leaderboard results on the blind test set are reported in Table 2. Several patterns emerge. First, discriminative taggers consistently outperform generative VLMs on Pearson calibration (SpanCalib 0.369 vs. Qwen 0.285), confirming that the MSE calibration head learns better-calibrated probabilities than autoregressive decoding. Second, the generative VLM achieves higher hallucinatedsample IoU (0.182 vs. 0.155), reflecting its superior span recall through deliberative reasoning. Third, the ensemble exploits both strengths: Qwens span proposals raise IoU while SpanCalibs probabilities improve calibration.

sections.title: Task Submissions
sections.content: We evaluate SpanCalib-VLM across four language splits: English (EN), French (FR), Italian (IT), and Chinese (ZH). Table 2 reports official shared task submission scores evaluated on the hidden test set. Table 7 provides detailed cross-lingual breakdown comparing base models against SpanCalib-VLM. SpanCalib-VLM demonstrates strong crosslingual generalization. On Chinese (ZH), the model achieves an impressive 0.437 Overall IoU and 0.958 Clean IoU, outperforming base Qwen-3.5-4B by +0.169 IoU. This higher Chinese performance stems from toideographic Chinese kenization granularity: Table 1: Performance on the SHROOM-Visions English validation split. Our full hybrid system (SpanCalib-VLM) achieves the highest Pearson calibration correlation and overall IoU, outperforming standalone baselines and individual subsystems across all metrics at optimal decision thresholds.

sections.content: Table 3 shows that ensemble performance is remarkably stable across τ [0.25, 0.45], all yielding IoU 0.391. This robustness arises because the fusion score distribution is bimodal: characters inside VLM-proposed spans receive high ensemble scores while others receive low scores, with few samples near the decision boundary.

sections.title: 5.5 Ablation Study
sections.content: Table 10 isolates the contribution of each component. Union-Calibrated Fusion outperforms weighted averaging (+0.032 Pearson) and intersection (+0.061). Removing the MSE calibration loss causes the largest drop (0.095 Pearson), confirming that direct probability supervision is essential. The vision tower provides modest IoU improvement (+0.003) while maintaining identical ensemble calibration.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SpanCalib-VLM, hybrid framework that combines multimodal discriminative tagger with generative VLM via Union-Calibrated Fusion. On SHROOMVisions, the ensemble achieves Pearson 0.413 and IoU 0.391 with 91.3% clean accuracy, demonstrating that principled fusion of fast calibration with deliberative span detection is an effective strategy for hallucination detection in LVLMs.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: In this section, we explore some limitations that our setup might have. First, SpanCalib-VLM produces false positives on complex but correct language: elaborate descriptions, idioms, and rare but accurate visual details are sometimes flagged as hallucinations, particularly by the sequence tagger which relies on surfacelevel distributional patterns rather than visual grounding. Second, the 512-token input limit causes the system to miss hallucinations in long responses entirely; any hallucinated content beyond the truncation boundary is undetectable. Third, while calibration is strong overall (Pearson 0.413), hallucinated-span IoU remains low (0.196), indicating that the system still struggles to precisely localize hallucination boundaries at the character level. Fourth, while our model is trained on joint multilingual dataset (EN, FR, IT, ZH), hyperparameter selection and ensemble fusion thresholds were optimized primarily on the English validation split. Finally, the ensemble cannot detect hallucinations that both subsystems miss; if neither the tagger nor the generative VLM identifies span, fusion cannot recover it.

Dual-process cognitive theory distinguishes fast, intuitive pattern recognition (System 1) from slow, deliberative reasoning (System 2), paradigm increasingly operationalized to combine complementary strengths in artificial intelligence (Booch et al., 2020; Li et al., 2025). In sequence processing and multimodal detection, generative VLMs excel at open-ended contextual reasoning and span proposal generation (System 2), but incur high computational latency and poor probability calibration. Conversely, discriminative sequence taggers evaluate representations in single deterministic forward pass (System 1), providing low latency and wellcalibrated token probabilities. SpanCalib-VLM operationalizes this hybrid synergy by pairing discriminative tagger for probability calibration with generative VLM for candidate span proposal generation.
